mainTopic: When to cry out over drought, famine, and other disasters; parables about rain since the חורבן; the story of נקדימון בן גוריון
overview: This amud finishes the גמרא's definition of בצורת versus כפנא. רבי חנינא gives a test based on price and availability. רבי יוחנן adds that when people have no money, the community cries out immediately even if food is cheap. The גמרא then explains how rain can help plants but not trees, trees but not plants, or both but not the water pits. It also explains how a single downpour can fill the pits without helping anything that grows. ברייתות set deadlines and limits for sounding the alarm. They also extend it to deadly disease and locusts, and decide what happens in שביעית, including ספיחין that feed the poor. רבי אלעזר בן פרטא teaches that rain has been meager since the חורבן and illustrates four kinds of rain years with parables. Finally, a story begins about נקדימון בן גוריון, who borrowed water for the pilgrims and must repay it by a deadline. The officer's mockery continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Drought vs. famine: defined by how far food must travel
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a definition. If food must come from another river region, it is בצורת. If it must come from another province, it is כפנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: …that is a drought. If food must be brought from one province to another province, that is a famine.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the middle of a sentence. The גמרא is finishing its definition: needing food from a nearby region is called בצורת, and needing food from a whole other province is called כפנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words on the previous amud said that bringing food 'from river to river' (a nearby region) is בצורת. The farther you must go to find food, the worse the situation. So מדינתא אמדינתא, province to province, is the more severe level, כפנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Drought: food is scarce and expensive, but can still be found
Famine: the more severe state, where food is really unavailable
From province to province: food must be brought from far away

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts mid-sentence. The first word, בצורתא, finishes the earlier clause 'river to river'. It does not belong to the province clause that follows.

phrases.english: (that is) a drought.
phrases.notes: End of the previous clause: if food must be brought from one river region to another, that is a drought.

phrases.english: (If food must be brought) from one province to another province, that is a famine.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְדִינְתָּא אַמְּדִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a definition begun on the previous amud
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food brought from a nearby region means בצורת. Food brought from another province means כפנא.

steps.title: A second test for drought vs. famine: price and availability
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא says that grain at one סאה per סלע which can still be bought is בצורת. Grain at four סאה per סלע which cannot be found is כפנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי חנינא said: If a סאה of grain costs a סלע, but grain is available, that is a drought. If four סאה cost a סלע, but grain is not available, that is a famine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא gives a different way to tell בצורת from כפנא. His test looks at price and at whether food can actually be found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At one סאה per סלע, grain is very expensive, but people with money can still buy it, so this is only בצורת. At four סאה per סלע the price is much cheaper, but if no grain can be found, that is כפנא. The key factor is availability, not price.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume 'four for a סלע' is the expensive case. It is the cheaper price. It counts as כפנא only because the grain cannot be found.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said:
A se'a for a sela, and it is available, that is a drought.
phrases.notes: Expensive, but you can buy it.

phrases.english: Four (se'a for a sela) and it is not available, that is a famine.
phrases.notes: Cheap, but there is nothing to buy.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, price-based definition alongside the distance-based one
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If grain is available, even at a high price, it is בצורת. If grain is unavailable, even at a low price, it is כפנא.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: when money is scarce, cry out immediately
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן limits the earlier rule to times when money is plentiful and produce is expensive. When money is scarce, even if produce is cheap, the community cries out right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: They only taught this when money is cheap and produce is expensive. But when money is expensive and produce is cheap, they cry out about it immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן adds a limit. The rules about rising prices apply only when people have money. If people have no money, that is itself an emergency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier rules measure the crisis by the food supply. רבי יוחנן points out a different crisis: food is cheap, but people cannot afford even that. Such a case gets immediate התרעה, just like a famine.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They only taught this when…': limits a rule to a specific case
They cry out: public fasting and prayer in a crisis

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
They taught this only
at a time when money is cheap (plentiful) and produce is expensive,
but when money is expensive (scarce) and produce is cheap,
they cry out about it immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the scope of the price-based definitions
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When money is scarce, they cry out immediately even if produce is cheap.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the halacha cares about whether people can actually eat, not just about how much grain is on the market.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's memory of hunger in Tiberias
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן recalls that in טבריה, grain was cheap, yet many people were swollen from hunger because they did not have even an איסר.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said: I remember when four סאה sold for a סלע, and many were swollen from hunger in טבריה because they did not have even an איסר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רבי יוחנן's rule from something he saw himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grain cost four סאה per סלע, the cheap price, and still people were starving. They did not have even an איסר, a tiny coin. This proves that a lack of money can make a real famine.
steps.whatToRemember: A famine can exist even when food is cheap, if people have no money to buy it. In that case they cry out immediately.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yochanan said:
I remember when there stood (were sold)
four se'a for a sela,
and there were many swollen from hunger in Tiberias
because they did not have (even) an issar.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן נְהִירְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the previous step with an eyewitness account
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's rule that a shortage of money calls for immediate crying out
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's own memory of hunger in טבריה when grain was cheap

steps.title: Rain enough for plants but not trees, or for trees but not plants
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and explains the first two cases. Gentle rain alone helps plants but not trees. Heavy rain alone helps trees but not plants.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: rain fell for the plants but not for the trees. Granted, plants but not trees can happen, when gentle rain came and heavy rain did not. Trees but not plants can happen, when heavy rain came and gentle rain did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and shows that its first two cases are realistic. It begins with בשלמא ('granted'), which tells us these cases are easy and that a harder question is coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Gentle rain soaks the topsoil, which helps plants with short roots, but it does not reach deep tree roots. Heavy rain reaches the trees but damages or fails young plants. So rain can help one kind of growth and not the other.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Granted…': accepts the easy cases before asking about a hard one
You can find it: this case is possible in real life

phrases.english: (The Mishnah taught:) It fell for the plants but not for the trees.
Granted, (rain enough) for the plants but not for the trees,
you can find it when gentle rain came
and heavy rain did not come.
For the trees but not for the plants,
when heavy rain came and gentle rain did not come.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לַצְּמָחִים וְלֹא לָאִילָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Gentle rain alone helps plants. Heavy rain alone helps trees.

steps.title: Rain enough for plants and trees but not for the water pits
steps.stepSummary: Rain that helps both plants and trees but does not fill the pits happens when both kinds of rain fell, but not in large amounts.
steps.simpleTranslation: For both this and that, but not for cisterns, ditches, and caves: you can find it when heavy and gentle rain both came, but not in abundance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going with the 'granted' cases and explains the משנה's third case. This is the last easy case before the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both gentle and heavy rain fell, so plants and trees are fine. But the total amount was too small to fill the storage pits for the summer.

keyTerms.meaning: Ditches and caves, also used to store water

phrases.english: For this and for that (plants and trees),

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא לַבּוֹרוֹת וְלֹא לַשִּׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת —
phrases.english: but not for the cisterns, nor the ditches and caves,
you can find it when heavy and gentle rain came,
but it did not come in abundance.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָזֶה וְלָזֶה אֲבָל לֹא לַבּוֹרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of 'granted' cases
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both kinds of rain fell, but not enough of it to fill the pits.

steps.title: How can rain fill the pits but not help plants or trees?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about a ברייתא that describes the reverse case: rain that filled the pits but did not help plants or trees. How is that possible?
steps.simpleTranslation: But this that was taught in a ברייתא: it fell for the cisterns, ditches, and caves, but not for this or that. How can you find that?
steps.whatsHappening: Now comes the hard question that the 'granted' cases were setting up. If there was enough rain to fill the pits, it seems it should have watered the plants and trees too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's cases all made sense. The ברייתא's case seems impossible, because filling pits takes a lot of rain. The word אלא marks the switch from the easy cases to the difficult one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But this that was taught…': brings a ברייתא that is hard to explain
How can you find it? How could this happen?

phrases.english: But this that was taught (in a baraita):
It fell for cisterns, ditches, and caves,
but not for this or that (plants and trees),
how can you find it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the easy cases with a case that seems impossible
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's case of rain enough for pits but not for plants or trees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rain heavy enough to fill pits should also water plants and trees, so the case seems impossible.

steps.title: Answer: a single heavy downpour
steps.stepSummary: This happens when the rain comes all at once in a downpour. It fills the pits, but it runs off without helping plants or trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: When it came as a downpour.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by describing a real situation: a sudden flood of rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A heavy pour washes over the ground quickly and collects in the pits. It does not soak into the soil, so plants and trees get no benefit. The ברייתא's case is possible after all.

keyTerms.meaning: A downpour: rain pouring all at once

steps.whatToRemember: Each kind of rain helps something different. Gentle rain helps plants, heavy rain helps trees, a large amount fills the pits, and a single downpour fills the pits but helps neither plants nor trees.

phrases.english: When it came in a downpour.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲתָיא בִּשְׁפִיכוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of the previous step
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a realistic case that fits the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Enough rain for the pits must also be enough for plants and trees.
steps.terutzMaskana: A sudden downpour fills the pits but runs off without soaking into the ground.

steps.title: Deadlines for sounding the alarm over trees and water pits
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that we sound the alarm for trees until near פסח, and for pits, ditches, and caves until near סוכות. If there is no drinking water, we sound it immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: We sound the alarm over trees until near פסח, and over cisterns, ditches, and caves until near סוכות. If people have no water to drink, we sound the alarm right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that sets deadlines for crying out about a lack of rain. Trees and water pits each get their own deadline.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each need has its own season. After פסח, rain no longer helps trees, so there is no point crying out for them. Pits can still be filled until סוכות, when the rainy season starts again. Drinking water is a matter of life, so there is no waiting at all.

keyTerms.meaning: They sound the alarm (with fasting, prayer, and shofar blasts)
Cisterns, ditches, and caves, which are places that store rainwater

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties back to the earlier steps. Different kinds of rain help trees and pits differently, so each one has its own deadline.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
They sound the alarm over trees until near Passover,
over cisterns, ditches, and caves
until near the Festival (Sukkot).
phrases.notes: 'החג' with no other name usually means סוכות

phrases.english: And if they have no water to drink
they sound the alarm over them immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בִּפְרוֹס הַפֶּסַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the kinds of rain, the גמרא now gives the timing for crying out over each kind of need.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trees: alarm until near פסח. Pits, ditches, and caves: until near סוכות. No drinking water: alarm immediately.

steps.title: What does 'immediately' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what 'immediately' means for the drinking-water case.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is their 'immediately'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא stops to ask what 'immediately' means. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fasts for rain follow a fixed order of days. So 'immediately' could mean today, or it could mean as soon as the normal fast schedule allows. The question asks which one is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Of theirs, meaning how the Sages use the word

phrases.english: And what is their 'immediately'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵיזֶהוּ מִיָּד שֶׁלָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the word 'immediately' from Step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact timing that 'immediately' refers to.

steps.title: 'Immediately' means the next Monday-Thursday-Monday series
steps.stepSummary: 'Immediately' means starting right away on the regular fast cycle of Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
steps.simpleTranslation: Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question. 'Immediately' means we begin the fast series of שני וחמישי ושני without waiting through the usual earlier stages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even an emergency fast follows the set order of fast days. The difference is that here we do not wait for the usual deadlines. The fast series starts at once.

keyTerms.meaning: Monday (the second day of the week)
Thursday (the fifth day of the week)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Immediately' here does not mean 'today'. It means the next fast series begins right away, on its regular days.

phrases.english: Monday, Thursday, and Monday.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֵׁנִי וַחֲמִישִׁי וְשֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Immediately' means beginning at once with the regular שני וחמישי ושני fast series.

steps.title: The alarm is sounded only in the affected region
steps.stepSummary: For all of these cases, only the region that is suffering sounds the alarm.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for all of them, they sound the alarm only in their own region.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a limit on place. Only the district that lacks rain sounds the alarm, not places where rain is falling normally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A rain shortage is a local problem. Since the suffering is in one district, the public response belongs to that district. Other areas that are getting rain do not join in.

keyTerms.meaning: All of them (all the cases above)

phrases.english: And over all of them they do not sound the alarm
except in their own district.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל כּוּלָּן אֵין מַתְרִיעִין עֲלֵיהֶן אֶלָּא בָּאִפַּרְכִיָּא שֶׁלָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a rule about place to the timing rules in Steps 9-11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alarm over a rain shortage is sounded only in the district that is affected.

steps.title: Diphtheria: alarm only when it is deadly
steps.stepSummary: For an outbreak of אסכרא, we sound the alarm only if it is causing deaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: And diphtheria: when it causes death, they sound the alarm over it. When it does not cause death, they do not sound the alarm over it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves from rain to disease. It rules that a plague of אסכרא calls for an alarm only when people are dying from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The alarm is for real disasters. An illness that is not deadly does not reach that level. Once it kills, it counts as a public emergency.

phrases.english: And diphtheria:
when there is death from it,
they sound the alarm over it.
When there is no death from it,
they do not sound the alarm over it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַסְכָּרָא, בִּזְמַן שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מִיתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from rain shortages to another kind of disaster, a plague.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sound the alarm over אסכרא only when it is deadly.

steps.title: Locusts: alarm for any amount
steps.stepSummary: We sound the alarm over גובאי (locusts) even if only a few appear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they sound the alarm over locusts in any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא rules that locusts call for an alarm even when only a small number show up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the disease, which needs deaths before an alarm, locusts need no minimum amount. A few locusts are a sign that a large swarm is coming. Since they destroy crops so quickly, we act right away.

keyTerms.meaning: In any amount, even a tiny one

phrases.english: And they sound the alarm over locusts
in any amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַתְרִיעִין עַל הַגּוֹבַאי בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of disasters, adding locusts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sound the alarm over גובאי in any amount.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר adds grasshoppers
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that we also sound the alarm over חגב (grasshoppers).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: Even over grasshoppers.
steps.whatsHappening: A תנא disagrees with the first opinion. He adds grasshoppers to the list of things we sound the alarm over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion covers only גובאי, which implies that grasshoppers do not count. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says grasshoppers can also cause great damage when they swarm, so they also call for an alarm.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Even over the grasshopper.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הֶחָגָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with Step 14 by extending the rule to grasshoppers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, we sound the alarm over grasshoppers as well.

steps.title: Trees only in the six regular years; pits even in שביעית
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: we sound the alarm for trees only in the six regular years, but for water pits even during שביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: They sound the alarm over trees during the other years of the seven-year cycle. Over cisterns, ditches, and caves, even in the seventh year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the שמיטה cycle. It asks which needs still call for an alarm during שביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שביעית the land is not worked, so crying out over trees is not needed then. Water for drinking is needed every year, so the alarm for pits continues even in שביעית.

keyTerms.meaning: The years of the seven-year cycle

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
They sound the alarm over trees
in the other years of the seven-year cycle.

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַבּוֹרוֹת וְעַל הַשִּׁיחִין וְעַל הַמְּעָרוֹת
phrases.english: Over cisterns, over ditches, and over caves
even in the seventh year.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בִּשְׁאָר שְׁנֵי שָׁבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא that adds a time limit based on the שמיטה cycle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trees: alarm only in the six regular years. Pits, ditches, and caves: even in שביעית.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: trees too in שביעית, for the poor
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that we sound the alarm for trees even in שביעית, because the poor live off them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Even over trees in the seventh year, because they provide food for the poor.
steps.whatsHappening: A dissenting view adds trees to the שביעית alarm. The reason given is that poor people depend on the fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שביעית the fruit is ownerless, and the poor eat from it. If the trees fail, the poor lose their food. So even in שביעית, trees are still a real need worth crying out for.
steps.whatToRemember: The alarm depends on real, present need. Trees until פסח, pits until סוכות, drinking water right away. Only the affected region cries out. Deadly disease and any locusts also call for an alarm. In שביעית we still cry out for water, and according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל also for trees, because the poor depend on them.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even over trees in the seventh year,
because they provide food for the poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בַּשְּׁבִיעִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in Step 16 by extending the שביעית alarm to trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, we sound the alarm over trees even in שביעית, because the poor depend on them.

steps.title: Sounding the alarm over aftergrowths in the seventh year
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא repeats the first one's rulings and adds that we sound the alarm over ספיחין in שביעית, because they feed the poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: We sound the alarm over trees in the other six years of the cycle. Over cisterns, ditches, and caves, we sound it even in שביעית. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: even over trees. We sound the alarm over ספיחין in שביעית, because they provide food for the poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, separate ברייתא (תניא אידך) on the same topic. Its wording is almost the same as the one in steps 16–17, but it ends by applying the reason 'sustenance for the poor' to ספיחין in שביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא (steps 16–17) has רבן שמעון בן גמליאל give the reason 'food for the poor' for trees in שביעית. In this version רבן שמעון בן גמליאל just says 'even over trees', and the 'food for the poor' reason is attached to a new case, ספיחין: crops that grow by themselves in שביעית, which anyone may eat. Since the poor depend on them, a threat to them justifies an alarm.

keyTerms.meaning: Aftergrowths: crops that sprout by themselves from leftover seeds, without planting
The seventh year of the cycle, when fields are not farmed
Cisterns, ditches, and caves: places where water is stored

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that in שביעית the deciding question is who would be hurt. Once the poor depend on a crop, its loss counts as a real emergency.

phrases.english: Another baraita taught:
phrases.notes: Introduces a second, separate ברייתא. It is very similar to the one in steps 16–17 but differs at the end.

phrases.english: We sound the alarm over trees
in the other years of the seven-year cycle.

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַבּוֹרוֹת עַל הַשִּׁיחִין וְעַל הַמְּעָרוֹת
phrases.english: Over cisterns, over ditches, and over caves
even in the seventh year.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even over trees.
We sound the alarm over aftergrowths in the seventh year,
phrases.notes: This is the new ruling in this step.

phrases.english: because they provide sustenance for the poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הַסְּפִיחִין בַּשְּׁבִיעִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel version (תניא אידך) of the ברייתא in steps 16–17. It differs in applying the 'food for the poor' reason to ספיחין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We sound the alarm over ספיחין in שביעית, because the poor depend on them for food.

steps.title: Since the Temple was destroyed, rain has become meager
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא teaches that since the חורבן rain has been meager, and he lists four kinds of rain years.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא said: From the day the בית המקדש was destroyed, rain has become meager in the world. Some years have a lot of rain and some have little. Some years the rain falls at the right time, and some years it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new ברייתא. רבי אלעזר בן פרטא says rain has been meager since the חורבן and lists four kinds of rain years, which he will explain one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic, a general teaching about rain after the חורבן. The four kinds come in two pairs: amount (a lot or a little) and timing (on time or late). This step sets up the parables that come next.

keyTerms.meaning: Shriveled or meager; here, rain that is sparse and stingy

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata said:
From the day the Temple was destroyed
rains have become meager for the world.
There is a year whose rains are abundant,
and there is a year whose rains are scarce.
There is a year whose rains fall in their proper time,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין גְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן.
phrases.english: and there is a year whose rains do not fall in their proper time.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, moving from the laws of sounding the alarm to a general teaching about rain after the חורבן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the חורבן rain has been meager, and there are four kinds of rain years: abundant, scarce, on time, and not on time.

steps.title: Parable for a year when rain comes on time
steps.stepSummary: A year with rain on time is like a servant who gets his weekly food on Sunday: he can bake and eat it properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year with rain on time like? It is like a servant whose master gave him his food for the week on Sunday. His dough is baked properly and eaten properly.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא explains the first kind of year with a parable. When rain comes on time, it is like a servant who gets his weekly food at the start of the week.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting the food on Sunday gives the servant the whole week to prepare it calmly and use it well. In the same way, rain at the right time lets the crops grow properly, so the rain is used fully.

keyTerms.meaning: "To what is it comparable?" (a phrase that opens a parable)
The first day of the week (Sunday)
Properly, the way it should be

phrases.english: A year whose rains fall in their proper time
to what is it comparable?
To a servant whose master gave him his food portion
on Sunday (the first day of the week),
so his dough turns out baked properly,
and eaten properly.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the four kinds of rain years from step 19, starting with the on-time year.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain on time is like food given at the start of the week, which is prepared and used properly.

steps.title: Parable for a year when rain comes late
steps.stepSummary: A year with late rain is like a servant who gets his food on ערב שבת: the dough is rushed and not used properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year without rain on time like? It is like a servant whose master gave him his food on ערב שבת. His dough is not baked properly and not eaten properly.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the opposite parable. Late rain is like getting your food on ערב שבת, when there is no time to prepare it well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This parable mirrors the one before it, and the only change is the timing. Food that arrives at the last minute gets rushed, so the dough comes out bad. Rain that comes late also does not help the crops the way it should.

keyTerms.meaning: Friday, the day before שבת, when time is short

phrases.english: A year whose rains do not fall in their proper time
to what is it comparable?
To a servant whose master gave him his food portion
on Shabbat eve,
so his dough turns out baked improperly,
and eaten improperly.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין גְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite of step 20's parable: same servant, same food, but given too late.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Late rain is like food given at the last minute, which cannot be prepared or used properly.

steps.title: Parable for a year of abundant rain
steps.stepSummary: A year of abundant rain is like a servant given all his food at once: grinding one big batch wastes no more than grinding a small one.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year of abundant rain like? It is like a servant whose master gave him all his food at once. The millstones lose the same amount from a כור as from a קב, and the dough loses the same amount from a כור as from a קב.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now explains the abundant-rain year. It is like getting all your food in one go, so you can process it all in one efficient batch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every time you grind grain or prepare dough, a fixed amount is lost, whether the batch is big or small. If you do it once with a huge amount (a כור) instead of many times with small amounts (a קב), much less is wasted overall. Likewise, abundant rain falling together soaks the land fully and is used well.

keyTerms.meaning: A very large measure of grain (equal to 180 קב)
Literally "eats"; here it means loses or uses up as waste

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read אוכלת as the servant eating more. Here it means the amount lost in processing, which is the same whether the batch is big or small. That is why one large batch is efficient.

phrases.english: A year whose rains are abundant
to what is it comparable?
To a servant whose master gave him his food portion
all at once,
so the millstones grind away (as waste) from a kor
phrases.notes: The amount lost in grinding is fixed for each batch.

phrases.english: only what they grind away from a kav,
and the dough loses from a kor
only as much as it loses from a kav.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מְרוּבִּין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the timing pair (steps 20–21) to the amount pair, starting with the abundant-rain year.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Abundant rain is like receiving everything at once: one big batch loses no more than a small one, so nothing is wasted.

steps.title: A year of scarce rain is like a servant fed a little at a time
steps.stepSummary: The fourth rain year: scarce rain is like a servant who gets his food in tiny portions, so every small batch carries the full waste.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year of scarce rain like? It is like a servant whose master gives him his food little by little. The amount the millstones waste when grinding a whole כור, they waste on every single קב. And the amount of dough that sticks and is lost from a whole כור is lost from every single קב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי אלעזר בן פרטא's list with the fourth and worst kind of year, a year of scarce rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every time you grind or knead, a fixed amount gets lost: flour stays in the millstones and dough sticks to the bowl. If you work in tiny batches, you pay that loss over and over. Scarce rain works the same way: small amounts of rain mostly get used up and wasted, and little real benefit is left.

keyTerms.meaning: a large measure of grain (30 סאה)
a small measure (1/180 of a כור)

steps.whatToRemember: Four rain years: on time is good, late is rushed, abundant means one big batch with no extra waste, and scarce means waste over and over.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'the millstones grind from a קב what they grind from a כור' as being about how much flour comes out. It is about how much gets LOST. A small batch loses as much as a big one.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מוּעָטִין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה —
phrases.english: A year whose rains are scarce, what is it like?
To a servant whose master gave him
his food little by little.

phrases.aramaic: נִמְצְאוּ רֵיחַיִים מַה שֶּׁטּוֹחֲנוֹת מִן הַכּוֹר
phrases.english: It turns out that what the millstones take from a whole כור,
phrases.notes: Meaning the flour lost in the grinding.

phrases.english: they take from each קב.

phrases.aramaic: נִמְצֵאת עִיסָּה כַּמָּה שֶׁנֶּאֱכֶלֶת מִן הַכּוֹר
phrases.english: And it turns out that however much dough is lost from a כור,
phrases.notes: Dough that sticks to the kneading bowl.

phrases.english: is lost from each קב.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מוּעָטִין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 22: abundant rain is one big batch, while scarce rain is many small wasteful batches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scarce rain is mostly wasted, like grinding and kneading in tiny batches that each carry the full loss.

steps.title: Second parable: kneading clay with plenty of water
steps.stepSummary: Another way to explain abundant rain: it is like kneading clay with lots of water, so the water lasts and the clay comes out well.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: what is a year of abundant rain like? It is like a person kneading clay. If he has a lot of water, the water does not run out and the clay is kneaded well. If he has only a little water, the water runs out and the clay is not kneaded well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second parable, introduced with דבר אחר, to show why a year of abundant rain is a blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the earth is like clay that needs water to be worked properly. With plenty of water the soil is fully soaked and good, but with a little water the water is used up before the job is finished. This makes the same point as before about scarce rain, using a new picture.

phrases.english: Another explanation:

phrases.aramaic: בִּזְמַן שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מְרוּבִּין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה —
phrases.english: When a year's rains are abundant, what is it like?
To a person who kneads clay.
If he has a lot of water,

phrases.aramaic: מַיִם אֵינָן כָּלִין, וְהַטִּיט מְגוּבָּל יָפֶה.
phrases.english: the water does not run out, and the clay is kneaded well.
If he has only a little water,

phrases.aramaic: מַיִם כָּלִים, וְהַטִּיט אֵינוֹ מִתְגַּבֵּל יָפֶה.
phrases.english: the water runs out, and the clay is not kneaded well.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: בִּזְמַן שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מְרוּבִּין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different parable for the abundant-rain year from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Abundant rain soaks the earth properly, while a little rain is used up before it does its job.

steps.title: נקדימון בן גוריון borrows water for the pilgrims
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא story: in a drought during the רגל, נקדימון בן גוריון borrows twelve wells of water from an officer and promises water or silver by a set date.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Once all of Israel went up to Jerusalem for the festival, and there was no water to drink. נקדימון בן גוריון went to a certain officer and said: Lend me twelve wells of water for the pilgrims, and I will give you back twelve springs of water. And if I do not, I will give you twelve talents of silver. And the officer set him a deadline.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story, a ברייתא about a miracle of rain. This step sets the scene: the drought and נקדימון's risky deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקדימון is betting that rain will come and refill the wells before the deadline. If it does not, he owes a huge sum of silver. The rest of the story builds on this deadline.

keyTerms.meaning: a very wealthy man of Jerusalem
a talent of silver, a huge sum

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Once all of Israel went up
for the festival to Jerusalem,
and they had no water to drink.

phrases.aramaic: הָלַךְ נַקְדִּימוֹן בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן אֵצֶל הֶגְמוֹן אֶחָד,
phrases.english: נקדימון בן גוריון went to a certain officer

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: הַלְוֵינִי שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲיָינוֹת מַיִם
phrases.english: and said to him: Lend me twelve wells of water
for the pilgrims,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנִי אֶתֵּן לָךְ שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה עֵינוֹת מַיִם.
phrases.english: and I will give you back twelve springs of water.
And if I do not give them to you,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵינִי נוֹתֵן לָךְ שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה כִּכַּר כֶּסֶף,
phrases.english: I will give you twelve talents of silver.
And he set him a deadline.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: פַּעַם אַחַת עָלוּ כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָרֶגֶל לִירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from parables about rain to a story about a rain miracle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the story: נקדימון takes on a debt that only rain can repay by the deadline.

steps.title: Deadline morning: the officer demands payment
steps.stepSummary: The deadline day comes with no rain. In the morning the officer demands water or money, and נקדימון answers that the whole day is still his.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the deadline came and no rain had fallen, in the morning the officer sent to him: Send me either the water or the money you owe me. He sent back: I still have time; the whole day is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the deadline day arrives, and the officer starts pressing for payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקדימון points out that a deadline set for a day includes the whole day, so he is not late yet. This builds the tension, since time is running out and there is still no rain.

phrases.english: When the deadline arrived
and no rain had fallen,
in the morning he sent to him:

phrases.aramaic: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת
phrases.english: Send me either the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי זְמַן,
phrases.english: He sent back: I still have time;
the whole day is mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן וְלֹא יֵרְדוּ גְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from the deal to the deadline day.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The deadline lasts the whole day, so נקדימון is not yet in default.

steps.title: Noon and afternoon: the demands repeat
steps.stepSummary: At noon and again in the afternoon the officer demands payment, and each time נקדימון answers that there is still time left in the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: At noon he sent to him: Send me either the water or the money you owe me. He sent back: I still have time left in the day. In the afternoon he sent to him: Send me the water or the money you owe me. He sent back: I still have time left in the day.
steps.whatsHappening: The story repeats the same exchange twice more, at noon and in the afternoon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repetition shows the day slipping away while נקדימון stays calm and trusting. His answer at noon is shorter than his morning answer ('I still have time left in the day' instead of 'the whole day is mine'), and he gives the same reply again in the afternoon.

phrases.english: At noon he sent to him:

phrases.aramaic: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת
phrases.english: Send me either the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי שְׁהוּת בַּיּוֹם.
phrases.english: He sent back: I still have time left in the day.
In the afternoon he sent to him:
Send me the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי שְׁהוּת בַּיּוֹם.
phrases.english: He sent back: I still have time left in the day.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּצָּהֳרַיִים שָׁלַח לוֹ: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the morning exchange at later hours to build tension.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נקדימון keeps holding to his right to the full day.

steps.title: The officer begins to mock נקדימון
steps.stepSummary: The officer ridicules נקדימון, starting to argue that it has not rained all year. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: That officer mocked him and said: The whole year no rain has fallen,
steps.whatsHappening: The story turns as the officer starts making fun of נקדימון. This line sets up the officer's full argument, which finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The officer's point is that if it has not rained all year, it surely will not rain in the few hours left. This mockery prepares the ground for the miracle that is about to come.

phrases.english: That officer mocked him and said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַשָּׁנָה כּוּלָּהּ לֹא יָרְדוּ גְּשָׁמִים,
phrases.english: The whole year no rain has fallen,

steps.triggerLanguage: לִגְלֵג עָלָיו אוֹתוֹ הֶגְמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After נקדימון's last reply, the officer responds with mockery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The officer is sure no rain will come; his statement continues on the next amud.
